topics.title: operator+ as a free function
topics.body: A free `operator+` takes both operands explicitly, so it works when the left operand is not the class type. Returning by value keeps the operands unchanged.

topics.title: operator<< returns the stream
topics.body: Returning `std::ostream&` lets `std::cout << p << " done"` chain, because each call feeds the same stream to the next. Returning void breaks every chained expression.

interview.answer: `::`, `.`, `.*`, `?:` and `sizeof`. Everything else that takes at least one class-type operand can be overloaded, though doing so should preserve the operator’s expected meaning.

interview.q: Why is `operator=` usually a member function?
interview.answer: It needs access to the object being assigned and must return `*this` by reference for chaining. The compiler-generated copy assignment is a member for the same reason.

mcq.q: What should `operator<<` for a stream return?
mcq.why: Returning the stream is what makes chained insertion work.
A free operator+ usually takes two const references.

topics.title: A function template instantiates per type
topics.body: The compiler generates a separate function for each deduced type, so `larger(3, 9)` and `larger(2.5, 1.5)` share source but not machine code. Errors appear at instantiation, not at definition.

topics.title: Non-type template parameters carry a value
topics.body: A template can take a constant value such as `int N`, which lets the size travel in the type. The array reference form below preserves the length instead of decaying to a pointer.

interview.q: Why must a template usually be defined in a header?
interview.answer: The compiler needs the definition to instantiate it for each type at the point of use. A definition hidden in a .cpp file is invisible to other translation units, producing link errors.

interview.q: What is the difference between a template and a macro?
interview.answer: A template is type-checked, scoped and instantiated by the compiler. A macro is textual substitution with no type safety, which is why templates replaced most macro-based generic code.

mcq.q: When is a function template type-checked?
mcq.why: Each instantiation is compiled for its concrete types.

mcq.q: What does `template <typename T, int N>` allow?
options: A type and a compile-time value
mcq.answer: A type and a compile-time value
mcq.why: `N` is a non-type parameter fixed at compile time.

topics.title: map keeps its keys sorted
topics.body: `std::map` orders keys by `operator<`, so iteration is sorted without an extra sort. Lookup is logarithmic and the container stores one value per unique key.

topics.title: unordered_map counts without promising order
topics.body: The hashed container gives average constant-time lookup, which is why it is the usual choice for frequency tables. Iteration order is unspecified, so never print it as if it were sorted.

interview.q: How do you choose between `map` and `unordered_map`?
interview.answer: Choose `map` when ordered iteration or range queries matter, and `unordered_map` when lookup speed is the priority and order is irrelevant. The hashed version needs a hash function and can degrade under bad hashing.

An operation that reallocates or restructures the container leaves existing iterators pointing at freed or moved storage. A vector push_back may invalidate all iterators, while a node-based map only invalidates the erased element’s iterator.

mcq.q: Which container keeps unique keys in sorted order?
mcq.why: A set stores unique keys ordered by the comparator.

mcq.q: What is the average lookup complexity of `unordered_map`?
mcq.why: Hashing gives average constant time, with worst case linear under collisions.

topics.title: sort with a lambda comparator
topics.body: The third argument is any callable that answers "does a come before b?". A lambda keeps the rule next to the call, and the sort stays stable only if `stable_sort` is used.

topics.title: accumulate needs the right seed type
topics.body: The initial value fixes the accumulator’s type. Seeding with `0` keeps integer arithmetic even when the range holds doubles, while `0.0` makes the average a real division.

interview.q: What is the difference between `find` and `binary_search`?
interview.answer: `find` scans linearly and works on any range, while `binary_search` assumes sorted input and halves the range. Use the latter when the data is already ordered and only presence matters.

interview.q: Why does `remove` not shrink a vector?
interview.answer: It moves the kept elements to the front and returns the new logical end, because it only sees iterators and cannot change the container. The erase-remove idiom removes the tail afterwards.

mcq.q: Which algorithm requires a sorted range?
mcq.why: Binary search depends on ordering to discard half the range.

topics.title: Throw by value, catch by const reference
topics.body: The exception object is copied when thrown and caught by reference avoids a second copy, while `const` prevents accidental modification. Catching by value slices derived exceptions.

topics.title: RAII cleans up during unwinding
topics.body: When an exception leaves a scope, every fully constructed local object is destroyed. That is why a guard object releases its resource even though the normal exit never runs.

interview.answer: That the function will not let an exception escape; if one does, `std::terminate` runs. It lets containers and the optimizer assume safety, which is why move constructors are usually marked noexcept.

interview.q: When should an exception not be used?
interview.answer: For expected, frequent conditions such as "not found" where a return value or `std::optional` is clearer and cheaper. Exceptions are for exceptional failure that the immediate caller cannot handle.

mcq.q: How should a standard exception be caught?
mcq.why: A const reference avoids slicing and an extra copy.

mcq.q: What happens if an exception leaves `main` uncaught?
mcq.why: An uncaught exception ends the program through terminate.

topics.title: A file stream closes at the end of its scope
topics.body: The `ofstream` destructor flushes and closes the file, so a nested scope is enough to make the write visible. Reading afterwards then sees the complete contents.

topics.title: filesystem splits a path
topics.body: `std::filesystem::path` understands separators, so `filename()` and `extension()` work on any platform instead of being hand-parsed from a string.

interview.q: Why check a stream after opening it?
interview.answer: A failed open leaves the stream in a failed state and every extraction returns immediately, so the program silently works with empty data. `is_open()` or a boolean test turns that into an explicit error path.

interview.q: What is the difference between text and binary mode?
interview.answer: Text mode may translate line endings on some platforms, while binary mode reads the exact bytes. Structured records should be read and written in binary with fixed layouts.

mcq.q: Which class writes to a file?
mcq.why: The output file stream opens for writing.

topics.title: optional expresses a value that may be missing
topics.body: `std::optional<T>` either holds a T or holds nothing, so "not found" needs no magic number. `value_or` supplies a default without a branch.

topics.title: Structured bindings walk a map
topics.body: Binding `[name, age]` to each map entry avoids the `first`/`second` noise, and the reference keeps the iteration from copying the pair.

interview.q: When is `std::optional` better than a sentinel like -1?
interview.answer: When every value of the type is legal, so no sentinel can be reserved. The type then states the possibility of absence and the compiler forces the caller to handle it.
It discards the untaken branch during instantiation, so a template can use operations that are valid for some types but not others. A plain `if` still has to compile both branches.

mcq.why: `optional`, `variant` and `any` each live in their own header.

mcq.q: What does `value_or(0)` do on an empty optional?
mcq.why: The fallback is returned when no value is stored.

topics.title: Binary search halves the range
topics.body: Sorted input lets each comparison discard half the remaining elements. The midpoint uses `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` so a large range cannot overflow the addition.

topics.title: Iterative Fibonacci is linear
topics.body: Keeping the last two values in a loop needs constant extra space and no call stack. The recursive version recomputes the same subproblems unless it is memoised.

interview.q: What is the time complexity of binary search and why?
interview.answer: O(log n), because every comparison halves the candidate range. A range of a million elements needs about twenty comparisons.

interview.q: When is a hash map preferable to sorting plus binary search?
interview.answer: When the data changes often and many lookups are expected, since a hash map gives average O(1) lookup without re-sorting. Sorting wins when ordered traversal or range queries are also needed.

mcq.q: Which precondition does binary search require?
mcq.why: The halving step is only valid on ordered data.

mcq.q: What is the complexity of iterative Fibonacci for n terms?
mcq.why: The loop performs one constant-time step per term.

topics.title: A thread must be joined or detached
topics.body: A `std::thread` that is still joinable when destroyed calls `std::terminate`. `join` waits for it; detach would let it run independently, which is rarely what a program with shared state wants.

topics.title: atomic removes the lost update
topics.body: A plain int incremented from two threads is a data race: read, add and write can interleave. `std::atomic<int>` makes the increment one indivisible operation, so the total is exact.

interview.answer: Two threads access the same memory concurrently, at least one writes, and no synchronization orders them. The result is undefined behaviour, not merely an unpredictable value.

interview.q: What does a mutex actually protect?
interview.answer: It protects the invariant that the locked region is supposed to maintain, not the variable by itself. Every access to the shared state must take the same lock or the protocol is broken.

mcq.q: What happens when a joinable `std::thread` is destroyed?
mcq.why: The destructor cannot leave a running thread unowned.
The operation completes as one unit with respect to other threads.
